utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Together. Together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so Ivo was left in the forest, Goran was left there --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- your son?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Igor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Ivo and Goran had weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't look. I was afraid, so I went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just been advised that it's 10.30. I'm happy to break here or happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have many more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Probably about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So let's have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think we left off last time when you said that you arrived in Anto Bralo's house on the 16th of April, for your personal safety. Was Anto Bralo there when you arrived at the house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how old was Anto Bralo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: He's 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he in camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see him in the possession of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were at Anto Bralo's house for most of the day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Anto Bralo left the house throughout that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Anto Bralo have a moustache?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to -- at the end of the day, I think you stated that you went back to your house and Goran advised you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was at your house when you arrived back there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did someone advise you to go back to Anto Bralo's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: It was Goran Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And he was at your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, he was not. He came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: He came where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: He came to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was he with anyone when he came to your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had been in the wood -- I mean, he was still in the wood with my Igor during the night, and then they came to the shelter. Because they were under-age children at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many days did you stay at Anto Bralo's shelter, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: For about five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think you said that you went back to your house every night of those five or six days.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Because there was a lot of shooting, my husband was at work, and I was alone, and I didn't feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the reason for going back to your house every night?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to see the cattle. I had some cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So during the days, you're not able to say what was happening at your house and other people's houses in the area of Dragan Papic's house and your other neighbours' houses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was at the shelter, and I didn't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you said that you went to the Radak Bridge every morning to get water.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you do that every morning, or did you do that most mornings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, occasionally I would go there. I wanted to help the woman who was at that house. That's why I went to get water every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that when you went to the bridge, you saw Ivo Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And which side of the bridge was he on? Was he on the Santici side, or the Donja Rovna side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: The Santici side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you said you didn't recognise anyone else on the Santici side.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: There was another person with him, but I don't know his name. Someone unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Dragan Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned a person by the name of Nusret Paco?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: A person that Dragan was friendly with. I think you said that Dragan and Nusret assisted each other prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how Nusret assisted Dragan?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: It was the other way around, because Nusret was a refugee, and he had a small child, and the food was not adequate. His conditions were not very good. And Dragan was better off, and he showed his understanding. He helped him. I helped him too, and so did Dragan's mother and everyone else. Nusret was a human being also, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did Nusret assist Dragan with his repair of cars?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes he did. Actually, I wouldn't know that. I didn't know what they did when Nusret came to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Nusret was killed in the conflict in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that Ivo Papic buried him, and his mother came over that morning, and I think it was the morning of the 16th of April. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. She came -- I'm not sure whether it was on that morning, but she came to me. She cried. She wanted to -- her son to be given a proper burial, and I was crying with her too. I was very sorry that such a thing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But it was in the morning that Mrs. Paco came to your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning, and me and my son were at home. It was very early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you're not sure whether it was the 16th or the 17th of April, the second or first --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I'm afraid I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From what you've said to the court today, it couldn't have been the 16th of April because you left your house at 5.30 in the morning and went to the wood, straight to Anto Bralo's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So it had to be at the 17th of April or the day after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: The following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you were mistaken when you said it was the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think Nusret's mother is Hankija Paco. That's her first name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Hankija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you've said to the court that you went to the Radak Bridge in the morning and then it was only in the evening that you went back to your house for the four or five days after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for about five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: However, there was one morning that you were at your house the day that Hankija Paco came over.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that morning I came to my house and Hankija came to my house as well. It was very early in the morning. I wanted to go to my house when there was still fog.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think Hankija Paco arrived at your house, and you were quite concerned about your safety when she arrived, the fact that a Muslim was at your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why were you concerned about your safety because Hankija Paco arrived? Was it because she was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't have any doubts about her at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, not you personally, but the fact that a Muslim was at your house the following day. Did that cause you some concern that if others, other HVO soldiers, found a Muslim at your house, that could have put you in some sort of trouble?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I even told Anto Bralo -- I mean, I asked Hankija whether there was anyone at their home, and she said yes, that the whole of her family was there. And I asked her whether I could tell any HVO member that they were there, and she said that it was okay and that she said that they were safe. They were escorted to safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you say to her, when she arrived, "Why did you come here? They might kill you now."

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I understood her as a mother. She wished that her son had proper burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was she concerned about her children, Hankija, when she arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She told me that I could say that they were all at home. I asked her whether I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you or your son tell her that she should hide her children?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I simply asked her whether they were armed and she said that they were not. Her children were no longer very young, they were adults.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Ivo Papic come to your house when Hankija Paco arrived there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. She told that to me, and on the way to my house she met Ivo and she asked him as well that her son be given proper burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Didn't initially Ivo say that he couldn't bury your son -- sorry, Hankija's son?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he told her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when was her son buried?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is was two days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There was a large group of refugees that lived near your house, with the surname Paco; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how big was that family group, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that there were at least 15 or 16 of them. They lived in three houses in my vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And a significant number of them were killed on the 16th of April, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you know of Fehim Paco?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Zaim Paco?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Huso Paco?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the father? No. No, I don't know him. I was closest with Nusret and his family, his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Alija Sesef, he was a neighbour to the Paco's; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And he was killed on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to another Alija, an elderly man, but I wouldn't know this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware that about six of that group that lived in those houses, those refugees houses, were killed on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can just go back for a moment to the first conflict when the Muslims were invited back by the Croats. I think you said that the Muslims from Gornji Ahmici came back first about three days later, and then the Muslims from perhaps the lower area of Ahmici came, returned after that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that they were immediately invited back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that Ivan Santic, which was -- I think is your uncle, the mayor of Vitez --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- he was involved in trying to organise that the Muslims come back to the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What other figures -- what other political or military figures from Vitez were also involved in the invitation or the organising that the Muslims come back to their houses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I just know Ivan Santic because he's a close relative of mine, and I don't know anything about any other political figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of Pero Skopljak's involvement from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I know Pero, but I don't know anything about his role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of Mario Cerkez's role? Do you know Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know him. I've heard about him, but I don't know anything about him or his role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of any conditions or arrangements that were put in place to allow the Muslims to come back? And when I refer to that I'm talking about the surrender, the Muslims surrendering their weapons as a condition of them coming back to the village. Are you aware of that type of condition being in place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at a local level, at the Ahmici-Santici level, who were the main organisers or negotiators that transmitted the invitation for the Muslims to come back? Who from the village guard was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was involved in that. I said that they'd been self-organised. There were very few of us. Even I once participated in the village guard. It was matter of self-organisation. People agreed amongst themselves what best suited them, and that's how I know that there was no single person who was an organiser. There were no orders. We would agree amongst ourselves as to who would stand guard, so I cannot tell you anything about any organiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But Nenad Santic was an organiser in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: He lives far away from me, so I don't know what exactly he did. I know what happened in my vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had seen Dragan Papic wearing black -- a black uniform that was given to him, and you also mentioned that he was wearing a camouflage uniform prior to the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you said that he told you that gave him a sense of importance.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, the camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware that he served on the front lines prior to the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. He was employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So if someone said that he worked at the frontlines prior to the 16th of April, are you saying they would be incorrect or that you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that prior to the 16th he was employed and he had a very responsible position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in your view, it's highly unlikely that he ever went to the frontlines prior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: "I can claim this with responsibility."

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: There was no front line at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned that Dragan or -- sorry, I withdraw that -- a flag would be hoisted on the house of Ivo Papic, a Croatian flag, prior to the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, most of the time it was a Croatian flag. Depending on the holiday, but for a religious holiday it would be a Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in terms of ethnic communities, that's where the Papic household and Dragan Papic, more specifically, sympathies lied, with the Croatian community in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: With the Muslim community as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he hang a Muslim flag -- sorry, was the Muslim flag hung from the -- from Ivo Papic's house, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I just know that Muslims celebrated their Bajram in the same way that we celebrated ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think you stated that other people in the village would hoist flags, or other Croats would hoist Croat flags from their houses. Can you tell the Court which other Croat households in Ahmici or Santici raised Croatian flags in 1992 before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about 1992. Slavko Milicevic would also fly a Croat flag. I would have done the same if I'd had one but I didn't. Other people did as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know the names of those households of other people that did it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll only ask one last question on this, Your Honour. You said that other people in your village raised flags and put them on their houses. I'm asking you, do you know the names of the households of the Croats that did that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: As I told you, Slavko Milicevic did, Dragan Papic, and again, I can say that I would have done the same if I had had one. Everybody who had a flag did the same, but mostly for religious holidays, for weddings, for example, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milicevic, I only have a few questions for you. In your opinion, was that some sort of a crime if the Croats hoisted their own flags on their houses during their holidays and the Muslims hoisted their flags during their holidays? In your opinion, is that an offence or crime?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Isn't it something quite normal and customary?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Customary. I respect the flag of any nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Let us make something clear regarding the date when your husband, before the conflict or during the conflict, I'm not sure, because the record differs on this point -- in one place it is stated that your husband went to work on the 16th of April, and in another place it says the 15th of April. That would be on the eve of the conflict. When, in fact, did your husband go off to work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly on the 15th of April, in the morning (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: So on the 16th of April, when you heard the gunfire, was your husband at home or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hear that it says "in the morning," that the husband went to work in the morning, but according to what the witness said, he went to work in the evening of the 15th of April. It says the 15th "in the morning," but he went on the 15th in the evening. He worked in the night-shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we will put the record straight, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask you once again, you said you were in Anto Bralo's shelter for a few days. You also said that every day you would drop by to see your house. Let me ask you once again: Why did you go to visit your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I simply went to see how things were and to feed the livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the exact date or are you perhaps are not sure when Nusret Paco was buried?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You think it was the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA MILICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Puliselic. We have no questions. Mrs. Milicevic, we are most grateful for you coming to give evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We gather that -- actually, we have been given an appeal -- a motion for appeal filed by Counsel Puliselic, and in view of this motion I think it's only proper for us to stay the proceedings until Judge May is back. I think it's most likely that he will not be able to come back tomorrow because he's still ill, so we will resume our proceedings on Monday, and depending on what the Appeal Chamber decides, or the bench of three Judges, we will see what to do with the three witnesses we have heard these days. It will be for the Appeal Chamber to decide. For the time being, I'm very sorry because we are wasting a day, a full day plus an hour today, but I think this is the only proper course of action. Any comments? Prosecutor, no comment? All right. So we will let you know whether by any chance Judge May is able to come tomorrow, attend our proceedings tomorrow. As I say, I doubt it, but through the Registry we will let you know I hope around, say, 4.00 this afternoon, so that you may know whether we will sit here in court tomorrow. Otherwise, we will resume our proceedings on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: at 11.35 p.m. sine die.
